summary:
We developed "Abandoned but Not Forgotten", an interactive website that tells the stories of 75 NASA spacecraft left on and around the Moon and Mars: landers, rovers, impact sites, orbiters and flyby probes, from Ranger and Apollo to Curiosity, Perseverance and Artemis II.
Users spin realistic 3D globes built from NASA imagery and click on spacecraft placed at their real landing or impact coordinates. Each one tells its story: why it was sent, what science it made possible, why it stopped working and what is happening to it today. Interactive 3D models with labelled parts, NASA diagrams, photos of landing sites from orbit, rover routes, a size comparison with a person and a quiz turn engineering and planetary science into something students can see and explore.
The project is designed for school-age space enthusiasts aged 10–16, as well as teachers and families, and works in English and Ukrainian. As new missions return to the Moon, these historic sites risk being damaged or forgotten. Protection starts with knowing they exist, and our website helps a new generation discover this shared heritage.
details:
LINKS

Source code (GitHub): https://github.com/nasaabandonedbutnotforgotten-alt/abandonedbutnotforgotten

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

"Abandoned but Not Forgotten" is an interactive web atlas of 75 NASA spacecraft left on and around the Moon (49) and Mars (26): landers, rovers, impact sites, orbiters and flyby probes, from Ranger 4 (1962) to Artemis II (2026). Users choose a world and spin a realistic 3D globe built from NASA imagery. Every spacecraft sits at its real landing or impact coordinates. Clicking it opens a story card: when it launched and arrived, why it was sent, what it discovered, why it stopped working, where it is now and a live "silent for…" counter. Each card adds:

- an interactive 3D model with labelled parts (50 models built from NASA engineering diagrams)

- NASA photos and labelled diagrams in a full-screen viewer

- "From orbit" images of the landing site today (LRO/LROC, MRO/HiRISE)

- real rover traverses of Curiosity, Perseverance and Opportunity

- a size comparison with a person, fun facts and links to NASA sources

A timeline replays the history of exploration year by year, and a quiz lets students test what they learned.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The site is designed for school students aged 10–16, teachers and families. It turns scattered NASA archives into one visual, story-based place where young people can see what is really out there and understand the engineering and science behind each machine. Teachers can use it as a ready-made lesson on space history and planetary science. As new missions return to the Moon, historic sites such as the Apollo landing areas risk being damaged. We want a new generation to know these places exist and to see them as shared human heritage worth protecting.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript: a static website with no backend and no frameworks

- Canvas 2D: our own per-pixel sphere renderer for the Moon and Mars globes, using NASA texture maps

- CSS 3D transforms and Canvas: lightweight interactive spacecraft models

- Python (Pillow, Tesseract OCR, Playwright): image processing, translating labels on NASA diagrams, automated testing

- VS Code with Live Server for development; Cloudflare Workers for hosting

- AI assistants: Claude (Anthropic) for coding, 3D models and translation; Gemini (Google) and Grok (xAI) for research, brainstorming and text checks

No special hardware was needed. Everything runs in a normal web browser on a laptop, tablet or phone.

CREATIVITY

Instead of dots and data tables, every machine "speaks" for itself through a short story. We rebuilt each spacecraft as a 3D model from NASA drawings, showed what its landing site looks like from orbit today and compared its size with a person, so abstract numbers become something a child can picture. The "silent for…" counter and the timeline turn history into something alive. The whole site, including the 3D models and NASA diagrams, works in both English and Ukrainian.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: every fact, date and coordinate is taken from NASA sources, which are linked in each card.

- Age-appropriate language: short sentences, simple words, no jargon.

- Performance: the site works on ordinary school computers without plugins or heavy 3D libraries.

- Accessibility: Ukrainian students can explore it in their own language.

- Respect for heritage: we focus on why these sites matter and why they should be protected.
